subject: Physics
title: Translatory Motion
learningOutcomes: Derive the three equations of motion for uniform acceleration from the definitions of velocity and acceleration and graphically.
Solve straight-line problems with constant acceleration using v_f = v_i + at, S = v_i t + ½at² and 2aS = v_f² − v_i².
Solve problems of bodies falling in a uniform gravitational field without air resistance (a = g).
Resolve the equations of motion into vertical and horizontal components for two-dimensional motion.
Explain that the horizontal component of a projectile’s velocity is constant.
Explain that the acceleration of a projectile is vertical and equal to that of a vertically free-falling object.
Explain that the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent of each other.
Find how high a projectile goes, how far it lands, where it is after a given time and how long it stays in the air.
Find the launch angle that gives the maximum range, and the relation between two launch angles that give the same range.
Predict qualitatively how air resistance affects the velocity components and so the range of a projectile.
State and apply the principle of conservation of momentum to simple one- and two-dimensional problems.
Explain karate chops, car crashes, ball and bat, explosions, the cannon and rocket thrust using momentum conservation.
Predict and analyse elastic collisions using conservation of kinetic energy and relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation.
Justify why the momentum of a closed system is always conserved while its kinetic energy may change.

sections.heading: Uniform Acceleration and the Equations of Motion
sections.body: A body has uniform acceleration when its velocity changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time. For straight-line motion with constant acceleration three equations link the initial velocity v_i, the final velocity v_f, the acceleration a, the time t and the distance S: v_f = v_i + at, S = v_i t + ½at² and 2aS = v_f² − v_i². The first has no S, the second has no v_f, and the third has no t, so the unwanted quantity decides which equation to use. They hold only while the acceleration stays constant.

sections.heading: Deriving the Equations from the Velocity–Time Graph
sections.body: On a v–t graph a straight line from v_i to v_f in time t shows uniform acceleration. The slope of the line is the acceleration, a = (v_f − v_i)/t, which rearranges to the first equation. The area under the line is the distance. That area is a trapezium, S = ½(v_i + v_f)t, and putting v_f = v_i + at gives the second equation. Eliminating t between the first equation and the area formula gives the third equation.

sections.heading: Sign Convention and Retardation
sections.body: Choose one direction as positive, normally the direction of the initial velocity, and give every quantity along it a plus sign and every quantity against it a minus sign. A body that is slowing down has an acceleration opposite to its velocity; this negative acceleration is called retardation. A body at rest at the start has v_i = 0, and a body that comes to rest has v_f = 0. For a braking car, putting v_f = 0 in the third equation gives the stopping distance S = v_i²/2a in size.

sections.heading: Free Fall
sections.body: A body moving under gravity alone, with air resistance neglected, is in free fall. Its acceleration is the same for every body, g = 9.8 m s⁻² directed downward, whatever the mass. The equations of motion apply with a = +g for a downward fall and a = −g for upward motion. A dropped body has v_i = 0, so v_f = gt, h = ½gt² and v_f² = 2gh. A ball thrown upward slows by 9.8 m s⁻¹ every second, stops at the top, and returns with the same speed at the launch level.

sections.heading: Vertical Throw: Height and Time
sections.body: For a ball thrown straight up with speed v_i, the velocity is zero at the top, so the maximum height is H = v_i²/2g and the time to reach it is v_i/g. The fall takes the same time as the rise, so the total time of flight is 2v_i/g. At the top the velocity is zero but the acceleration is still g downward, which is why the ball does not stay there.

sections.heading: Motion in Two Dimensions and Components
sections.body: When motion is not along a line, the velocity is resolved into a horizontal component v_i cosθ and a vertical component v_i sinθ, where θ is the angle with the horizontal. The equations of motion are then written separately for the x- and y-directions, with time as the only quantity common to both. Because the two directions are at right angles to each other, each can be solved on its own.

sections.heading: Projectile Motion
sections.body: A projectile is a body thrown into the air that moves under the force of gravity alone. Its path, the trajectory, is a parabola. The horizontal motion has no acceleration, so the horizontal velocity v_i cosθ stays constant. The vertical motion has the constant downward acceleration g, exactly like free fall. The two motions are independent: they share only the time, so a ball dropped from rest and a ball thrown horizontally from the same height hit the ground together.

sections.heading: Horizontal Launch
sections.body: A body thrown horizontally with speed v_i from a height h starts with no vertical velocity. The vertical motion is a free fall from rest, so the time of flight is t = √(2h/g). The horizontal distance covered is x = v_i t. On landing the vertical velocity is gt and the horizontal velocity is still v_i, so the landing speed is √(v_i² + (gt)²) and it makes an angle tan⁻¹(gt/v_i) below the horizontal.

sections.heading: Projectile Launched at an Angle
sections.body: For a launch at angle θ on level ground, the vertical velocity at the top is zero, so the time to the top is v_i sinθ/g and the time of flight is T = 2v_i sinθ/g. The maximum height is H = v_i² sin²θ/2g. The range is R = (v_i cosθ)T = v_i² sin2θ/g. At any time t the position is x = (v_i cosθ)t and y = (v_i sinθ)t − ½gt². At the highest point the velocity is purely horizontal and equals v_i cosθ.

sections.heading: Maximum Range and Equal Ranges
sections.body: Since R = v_i² sin2θ/g and the largest value of sin2θ is 1, the range is greatest when 2θ = 90°, that is θ = 45°, and then R_max = v_i²/g. Two launch angles θ and (90° − θ) give the same range because sin2θ = sin(180° − 2θ). Such angles are complementary. The smaller angle gives a lower, faster path and the larger angle gives a higher path that takes longer.

sections.heading: Effect of Air Resistance
sections.body: Real projectiles are slowed by the air. Air resistance acts opposite to the velocity, so both the horizontal and the vertical components of the velocity are reduced, and the horizontal velocity no longer stays constant. Energy is lost to the air. As a result the range and the maximum height become smaller than the ideal values, and the path is no longer a symmetric parabola: it falls more steeply than it rose.

sections.heading: Linear Momentum and Its Conservation
sections.body: The linear momentum of a body is the product of its mass and velocity, p = mv. It is a vector with the direction of the velocity and the SI unit kg m s⁻¹. For an isolated system, where no net external force acts, the total momentum before an interaction equals the total momentum after it. For two bodies, m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂. Momentum in each perpendicular direction is conserved separately, which is how two-dimensional collisions are solved.

sections.heading: Applications of Momentum Conservation
sections.body: A gun and its bullet start at rest, so the total momentum is zero; the bullet goes forward and the gun recoils backward with equal and opposite momentum, giving v_gun = −m_bullet v_bullet/m_gun. A rocket moves forward because it throws burning gas backward at high speed. A karate expert stops the hand in a very short time so the force on the tile is large. A car with a crumple zone takes longer to stop, so the force on the passengers is smaller.

sections.heading: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
sections.body: In every collision of an isolated system the total momentum is conserved. In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy is also conserved, and the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation. In an inelastic collision some kinetic energy changes into heat, sound or deformation. In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together and move with a common velocity v = (m₁u₁ + m₂u₂)/(m₁ + m₂), and the loss of kinetic energy is the largest possible.

sections.heading: Why Kinetic Energy Can Change but Momentum Cannot
sections.body: Momentum is conserved because the forces the colliding bodies exert on each other are equal and opposite, so their momentum changes cancel. Kinetic energy has no such rule: it is a scalar, and the work done in deforming the bodies, or the energy released in an explosion, can lower or raise it. Total energy is always conserved, but kinetic energy alone is conserved only in elastic collisions such as those of billiard balls and gas molecules.

definitions.definition: Motion in which a body moves from one place to another, such as motion along a straight line or along a curved path in a plane.
The study of motion without considering its causes: displacement, velocity and acceleration.
Velocity changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time, so the v–t graph is a straight line.
The three relations between v_i, v_f, a, t and S that hold for straight-line motion with constant acceleration.
Negative acceleration: the body slows down.
Motion under gravity alone, with air resistance neglected, so a = g = 9.8 m s⁻² downward.
The constant downward acceleration g of every freely falling body near the Earth’s surface.
A body thrown into the air that then moves under gravity alone; its path is a parabola.
The curved path followed by a projectile.
v_icosθ; stays constant because there is no horizontal acceleration.
v_isinθ at launch; changes by g every second.
The greatest vertical distance H reached; vertical velocity is zero there.
The total time T a projectile stays in the air before returning to the launch level.
The horizontal distance R from the launch point to the landing point at the same level.
A frictional force of the air on a moving body that reduces its energy and speed.
The product of mass and velocity, p = mv; a vector.
A system on which no net external force acts.

A collision in which both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.

examTips: Before choosing an equation of motion, write the known and unknown quantities; pick the equation that has no unwanted quantity (no S, no v_f or no t).
Fix the positive direction first. For an upward throw take up as positive, so a = −g; for a downward fall take down as positive, so a = +g.
At the highest point of a projectile the vertical velocity is zero but the acceleration is still g; for an angled launch the speed there is v_i cosθ, not zero.
For a horizontal launch the vertical motion starts from rest. Use t = √(2h/g) first and only then find the horizontal distance.
Range formulas R = v_i² sin2θ/g and R_max = v_i²/g hold only when the projectile lands at the launch level and air resistance is neglected.
Complementary angles give the same range; if the range is the same for 30° and another angle, the other angle is 60°.
In a momentum problem write the total momentum before and after with signs. A body moving the opposite way carries a negative momentum.

In an elastic collision use both momentum and kinetic energy (or relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation); in a perfectly inelastic collision use only momentum with a common velocity.
Always write the SI unit with the answer: m s⁻¹ for velocity, m s⁻² for acceleration, kg m s⁻¹ for momentum, J for energy.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which equation of motion does not contain the time t?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The third equation, 2aS = v_f² − v_i², links velocity, acceleration and distance without time.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A ball thrown vertically upward is at its highest point. Which statement is correct?

options: Its velocity is zero and its acceleration is g downward
Its velocity and acceleration are both zero
Its velocity is maximum and its acceleration is g
Its velocity is zero and its acceleration is g upward

practiceQuestions.explanation: At the top the velocity is zero for an instant, but gravity still acts, so the acceleration is g = 9.8 m s⁻² downward.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which component of the velocity of a projectile stays constant when air resistance is neglected?
practiceQuestions.explanation: There is no horizontal acceleration, so the horizontal component v_i cosθ stays constant; the vertical component changes by g every second.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m s⁻² for 5 s. How far does it travel?
practiceQuestions.explanation: S = v_i t + ½at² = 0 + ½(2)(5)² = 25 m.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A stone is dropped from the top of a 19.6 m tall building. How long does it take to reach the ground? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
A ball is launched at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above level ground. What is its range? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m s⁻¹ hits a 1 kg trolley at rest and they stick together. What is their common velocity?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Momentum is conserved: 2 × 3 = (2 + 1)v, so v = 6/3 = 2 m s⁻¹.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Two projectiles are launched with the same speed and have the same range. If one angle is 25°, what is the other?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Equal ranges occur for complementary angles that add up to 90°, so the other angle is 90° − 25° = 65°.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The total momentum of an isolated system is conserved in every type of collision.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Momentum is conserved in elastic and inelastic collisions alike because no net external force acts.

practiceQuestions.prompt: At the highest point of a projectile’s path launched at an angle, its velocity is zero.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Only the vertical component is zero there; the horizontal component v_i cosθ is still present.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy before and after the collision is the same.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved in an elastic collision.

practiceQuestions.prompt: For a projectile that lands at its launch level with no air resistance, the range is greatest at a launch angle of 45°.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. R = v_i² sin2θ/g is maximum when sin2θ = 1, that is θ = 45°.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The SI unit of linear momentum is ______.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Momentum p = mv, so its unit is kg × m s⁻¹ = kg m s⁻¹ (equivalent to N s).

practiceQuestions.prompt: In free fall near the Earth every body has an acceleration of ______ m s⁻² (number only).
practiceQuestions.explanation: The acceleration due to gravity is g = 9.8 m s⁻², the same for all freely falling bodies.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A 5 kg body moves at 4 m s⁻¹. Its momentum is ______ kg m s⁻¹ (number only).

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange the steps of finding the range of a projectile launched at an angle, starting with resolving the velocity.

items: Multiply v_i cosθ by the time of flight
Resolve v_i into v_i cosθ and v_i sinθ
State the range with its unit
Find the time of flight from the vertical motion
correctOrder: Resolve v_i into v_i cosθ and v_i sinθ
Find the time of flight from the vertical motion
Multiply v_i cosθ by the time of flight
State the range with its unit

sequencingActivity.explanation: The vertical motion gives the time of flight, and the constant horizontal velocity then gives the range: R = (v_i cosθ)T.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A ball is launched from level ground at 40 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Find its maximum height and its range. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: H = (v_i sinθ)²/2g = (20)²/19.6 = 20.4 m and R = v_i² sin2θ/g = 1600 × sin60°/9.8 = 141.4 m. The second option forgets the square on the sine in H.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A 4 kg gun fires a 0.02 kg bullet at 400 m s⁻¹. Find the recoil speed of the gun and the ratio of the kinetic energy of the gun to that of the bullet.
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Momentum: 4 v + 0.02 × 400 = 0, so |v| = 8/4 = 2 m s⁻¹. K_gun = ½(4)(2)² = 8 J and K_bullet = ½(0.02)(400)² = 1600 J, so the ratio is 8 : 1600 = 1 : 200. The light bullet carries almost all the kinetic energy.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m s⁻¹ collides head-on and elastically with a 4 kg ball at rest. Find the velocities of the two balls after the collision.
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Momentum: 12 = 2v₁ + 4v₂. Relative speed of approach (6) equals relative speed of separation: v₂ − v₁ = 6. Solving gives v₁ = −2 m s⁻¹ (the light ball bounces back) and v₂ = 4 m s⁻¹. Check: kinetic energy 36 J before and 4 + 32 = 36 J after.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ from the edge of a 44.1 m high cliff. Find the horizontal distance from the foot of the cliff and the speed with which it hits the ground. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: t = √(2h/g) = √(2 × 44.1/9.8) = 3 s, so x = 15 × 3 = 45 m. The vertical velocity is gt = 29.4 m s⁻¹, so v = √(15² + 29.4²) = 33 m s⁻¹. The horizontal velocity is not lost, so the speed is more than either component alone.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m s⁻¹ crashes into a stationary 3000 kg truck and the two vehicles move on together. Find their common speed and the kinetic energy lost.

options: 5 m s⁻¹ and no loss of kinetic energy

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Momentum: 1000 × 20 = 4000 v, so v = 5 m s⁻¹. Kinetic energy before = ½(1000)(20)² = 200 kJ; after = ½(4000)(5)² = 50 kJ. The loss of 150 kJ (75%) goes into deforming the vehicles, heat and sound, while momentum stays conserved.
